arXiv:2602.02061v1 [cs.LG] 02 Feb 2026

Learning to Route and Schedule LLMs from User Retrials via Contextual Queueing Bandits

Seoungbin Bae ††thanks: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineerin, KAIST sbbae31@kaist.ac.kr    Junyoung Son ††thanks: Graduate School of Data Science, KAIST jun.son@kaist.ac.kr    Dabeen Lee ††thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Seoul National University dabeenl@snu.ac.kr
Abstract

Explosive demands for LLMs often cause user queries to accumulate in server queues, requiring efficient routing (query-LLM matching) and scheduling (query prioritization) mechanisms. Several online algorithms are being deployed, but they overlook the following two key challenges inherent to conversational LLM services: (1) unsatisfied users may retry queries, increasing the server backlog, and (2) requests for “explicit" feedback, such as ratings, degrade user experiences. In this paper, we develop a joint routing and scheduling algorithm that leverages “implicit" feedback inferred from user retrial behaviors. The key idea is to propose and study the framework of contextual queueing bandits with multinomial logit feedback (CQB-MNL). CQB-MNL models query retrials, as well as context-based learning for user preferences over LLMs. Our algorithm, anytime CQB (ACQB), achieves efficient learning while maintaining queue stability by combining Thompson sampling with forced exploration at a decaying rate. We show that ACQB simultaneously achieves a cumulative regret of 𝒪~​(t)\mathchoice{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,\left(\sqrt{t}\right)}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})} for routing and a queue length regret of 𝒪~(t−1/4)\mathchoice{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,\left(t^{-1/4}\right)}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})} for any large tt. For experiments, we refine query embeddings via contrastive learning while adopting a disjoint parameter model to learn LLM-specific parameters. Experiments on SPROUT, EmbedLLM, and RouterBench datasets confirm that both algorithms consistently outperform baselines.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized various domains, driving explosive demands for LLM-based applications (Achiam et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023; Dubey et al., 2024). However, running LLMs is computationally intensive and resource-demanding. Therefore, a flood of user queries, coupled with limited server capacity, inevitably leads to significant query accumulation in system queues. Hence, efficient query routing and scheduling is crucial to ensure high-quality user experiences and system sustainability (Kwon et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2024).

To mitigate such system congestion, LLM routing and scheduling frameworks have emerged as necessary components. In a typical system of multiple LLMs with varying types and levels of capabilities, performance, and costs, the system must decide which model to serve a given query (routing) and in what order to process backlogged queries (scheduling) (Mitzenmacher and Shahout, 2025). The first approaches have relied on policies learned offline (Ong et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024), but these methods often fail to adapt to the dynamic and non-stationary nature of online environments. This limitation has motivated the adoption of online learning frameworks (Chiang et al., 2025; Jitkrittum et al., 2025), which learn optimal policies through sequential interactions with the environment.

However, existing online learning approaches are often limited in practice as they overlook two key challenges inherent to conversational LLM services. First, they fail to account for the subsequent impact of user dissatisfaction. When users encounter unsatisfactory responses, they often retry queries. This retrial behavior increases server backlog, exacerbating congestion. This introduces a trade-off between exploration and system stability: exploring potentially sub-optimal models may induce user retrials that increase queue length. Second, most algorithms rely on explicit user feedback (e.g., ratings, preference information) to update their policies. In practice, however, such feedback is sparse, as users are often reluctant to provide it. Furthermore, mandating explicit feedback can disrupt conversation flows and degrade user experiences.

In this paper, we address these challenges by presenting a novel formulation for the joint routing and scheduling problem via contextual queueing bandits with multinomial logit feedback (CQB-MNL). Specifically, CQB-MNL considers a discrete-time queueing system with NN LLMs, where in each round a query with some context information arrives at the queue. An algorithm for CQB-MNL chooses a pending query with the highest priority (scheduling) and recommends an assortment of KK LLMs for response generation (routing) (See Figure 1). Here, the case K=1K=1 corresponds to the standard single-response setting, which is essentially a dynamic matching problem. The case K=2K=2 represents the pairwise comparison setting, commonly employed to collect human preferences for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where a user receives two candidate responses and is asked to select one. In CQB-MNL, the choice behavior of a user is modeled with the multinomial logit (MNL) framework (Agrawal et al., 2019; Oh and Iyengar, 2019). Basically, the user accepts one of KK candidate responses, indicating satisfaction, or rejects all and retries the query, indicating dissatisfaction, and the choice decision is governed by the MNL model. This formulation enables the system to learn optimal policies based on implicit feedback inferred from user retrials.

However, an online learning algorithm for CQB-MNL requires exploration, which may involve suggesting suboptimal models, and as a result, it inherits the risk of triggering retrials, causing system congestion. Therefore, we need an algorithm that cleverly balances exploration and system stability. To address this requirement, we propose an algorithm, anytime CQB (ACQB), that achieves efficient learning of the underlying MNL model while maintaining queue stability. The main backbone of ACQB is Thompson sampling for MNL, while it enforces uniform exploration steps.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce CQB-MNL, a novel online learning framework designed to address the two critical challenges inherent to online learning for LLM routing and scheduling: system congestion due to user dissatisfaction triggering retrials and impracticality of relying on explicit feedback.

  • •

    We propose ACQB for CQB-MNL that allows efficient learning of the unknown MNL model while guaranteeing queue stability. In each time step, Thompson sampling or uniform exploration is performed. Here, the probability of running uniform exploration decreases as time goes on.

  • •

    ACQB is an “anytime" algorithm suitable for continuous LLM services. It works without prior knowledge of the time horizon or the traffic slackness parameter. These parameters are usually unavailable a priori.

  • •

    We establish that ACQB simultaneously achieves a cumulative regret of 𝒪~​(t)\mathchoice{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,\left(\sqrt{t}\right)}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(\sqrt{t})} for learning the MNL model and a queue length regret of 𝒪~(t−1/4)\mathchoice{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,\left(t^{-1/4}\right)}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(t^{-1/4})}, ensuring convergence to optimal queue length, for any large tt.

  • •

    For experiments, we employ disjoint parameterization to capture individual LLM-specific characteristics (Section 5.1). Moreover, we refine query embeddings via contrastive learning. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets (EmbedLLM, SPROUT, RouterBench) demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform baselines.

2 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formulate the online learning of LLM routing and scheduling with users’ retrials as a contextual queueing bandit problem. We consider a discrete-time queueing environment with a single queue and NN LLMs. At each round tt, a user query (together with its context) arrives and joins the queue. The agent then performs a joint operation: it selects a pending query to process from the queue (scheduling) and assigns an appropriate LLM (or an assortment of LLMs) to the selected query (routing). Formally, at round tt, the agent observes a queue state 𝒳t⊆𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, given by the set of contexts of the remaining queries, and chooses a query context xt∈𝒳tx_{t}\in\mathcal{X}_{t}. The corresponding feature vector of xtx_{t} for each LLM j∈[N]j\in[N] is denoted as xt,jx_{t,j} (or x−jx_{-j} for an arbitrary context xx). The agent then chooses an assortment of servers St∈𝒞S_{t}\in\mathcal{C}, where 𝒞:={S⊆[N]:|S|=K}\mathcal{C}:=\{S\subseteq[N]:|S|=K\} and KK is the assortment size. For simplicity, we fix KK throughout the paper; in practice, one may deploy a policy where the agent primarily uses a single LLM (K=1K=1) and occasionally generates two answers (K=2K=2) when additional feedback is required, and the same analysis applies.

We characterize user satisfaction through follow-up behavior. If the user is satisfied—specifically, accepting the answer in the single-response setting (K=1K=1) or selecting a preferred answer in the pairwise setting (K=2K=2)—the corresponding query departs the queue. Conversely, if the user is dissatisfied, they exhibit retrials, which we model as the query remaining, or re-entering the queue. We describe these dynamics formally as follows: Let Q⁡(t)=|𝒳t|Q(t)=|\mathcal{X}_{t}| denote the queue length at the beginning of round tt. Let A⁡(t)∈{0,1}A(t)\in\{0,1\} indicate the random arrival of a new job, and D⁡(t)∈{0,1}D(t)\in\{0,1\} denote the random departure at time tt. When A⁡(t)=1A(t)=1, we denote the context of the newly arriving job as x(t)x^{(t)}. The queue state then evolves as:

𝒳t+1=𝒳t∖{xt:D⁡(t)=1}∪{x(t):A⁡(t)=1},\displaystyle\mathcal{X}_{t+1}=\mathcal{X}_{t}\setminus\{x_{t}:D(t)=1\}\cup\{x^{(t)}:A(t)=1\},

and the queue length evolves according to Q⁡(t+1)=[Q⁡(t)+A⁡(t)−D⁡(t)]+Q(t+1)=[Q(t)+A(t)-D(t)]^{+}, where [z]+=max⁡{0,z}[z]^{+}=\max\{0,z\}. For technical convenience, if the queue is empty (Q⁡(t)=0Q(t)=0), the agent selects a dummy job x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and the resulting feedback is not used for learning.

We model the user choice probability using the MNL model (Agrawal et al., 2019; Oh and Iyengar, 2019). The agent observes a binary choice vector yt=[yt​0,yt​1,…,yt​K]∈{0,1}K+1y_{t}=[y_{t0},y_{t1},\dots,y_{tK}]\in\{0,1\}^{K+1}, where ∑j∈[K]∪{0}yt​j=1\sum_{j\in[K]\cup\{0\}}y_{tj}=1 and yt​j=1y_{tj}=1 if the user chooses the jj-th LLM in the assortment StS_{t}, and 00 otherwise. We designate the outside option (no choice) as yt​0=1y_{t0}=1, representing user dissatisfaction. The probability that a user chooses item jj from assortment SS given context xx is defined as pj​(x,S,θ∗)p_{j}(x,S,\theta^{*}), where θ∗∈ℝd\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unknown parameter, and pj​(x,S,θ):=exp⁡(x−j𝖳​θ)1+∑j′∈Sexp⁡(x−j′𝖳​θ)p_{j}(x,S,\theta):=\frac{\exp(x_{-j}^{\mathsf{T}}\theta)}{1+\sum_{j^{\prime}\in S}\exp(x_{-j^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\theta)} for j∈𝒮j\in\mathcal{S}, and p0​(x,S,θ):=11+∑j′∈Sexp⁡(x−j′𝖳​θ)p_{0}(x,S,\theta):=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j^{\prime}\in S}\exp(x_{-j^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\theta)} for the outside option (j=0j=0). We evaluate the performance of the agent using two key measures: (i) queue length regret and (ii) cumulative regret. Let π\pi denote the agent’s policy and π∗\pi^{*} denote the optimal policy that has prior knowledge of the true parameter θ∗\theta^{*}. Given a set of remaining features 𝒴⊆𝒳\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{X}, π∗\pi^{*} selects the query-assortment pair (x∗,S∗)(x^{*},S^{*}) that maximizes the expected departure rate, i.e., (x∗,S∗)∈arg​maxx∈𝒴,S∈𝒞⁡R​(x,S,θ∗)(x^{*},S^{*})\in\argmax_{x\in\mathcal{Y},S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*}). Rt:=𝔼⁡[Q⁡(t)−Q∗​(t)],\displaystyle R_{t}:=\mathbb{E}[Q(t)-Q^{*}(t)],

Accordingly, this metric simultaneously evaluates the routing and scheduling performance. Moreover, to evaluate the routing performance in terms of departure-rate optimality, we consider cumulative regret, a standard measure in the bandit literature. ‖x−j‖2≤1\|x_{-j}\|_{2}\leq 1 for all x∈𝒳,j∈[N]x\in\mathcal{X},j\in[N]. Also, ‖θ∗‖≤1\|\theta^{*}\|\leq 1.

Assumption 1 states that the norms of the feature vector x−jx_{-j} and the unknown parameter θ∗\theta^{*} are bounded. Assumption 2 introduces problem-dependent parameters that control the local behavior of μ˙​(⋅)\dot{\mu}(\cdot). Assumption 3 imposes a regularity assumption on the underlying distribution. Assumption 4 specifies a traffic slack condition to guarantee stability, which is standard in the queueing bandit literature (Krishnasamy et al., 2016; Bae et al., 2026).

3 Proposed Algorithm

In this section, we introduce our proposed algorithm, ACQB, which is illustrated in Algorithm 1. The algorithm consists of two branches: (i) random exploration and (ii) a Thompson sampling-based optimistic rule. Let E⁡(t)∼Bern⁡(η⁡(t))E(t)\sim\Bern(\eta(t)) be the random variable that indicates whether we run random exploration in round t+1t+1, where η(t)=min{1,c1(t+1)−1/2}\eta(t)=\min\{1,c_{1}(t+1)^{-1/2}\} is the exploration parameter for some absolute constant c1>0c_{1}>0. Then, in each round tt, if there is a new job arrival (A⁡(t−1)=1A(t-1)=1), we perform random exploration with probability η⁡(t−1)\eta(t-1) (i.e., when E⁡(t−1)=1E(t-1)=1) by selecting the newly arriving job x(t−1)x^{(t-1)} and choosing the LLM assortment in a round-robin manner. If this event (i.e., A⁡(t−1)=1A(t-1)=1 and E⁡(t−1)=1E(t-1)=1) does not occur, we choose the query-assortment pair according to the Thompson sampling-based optimistic rule (Oh and Iyengar, 2019): (Line 6) sample {θ~t−1(i)}i=1M\{\widetilde{\theta}^{(i)}_{t-1}\}_{i=1}^{M} from the Gaussian distribution N⁡(θ^t−1,αt−12​Vt−1−1)N(\widehat{\theta}_{t-1},\alpha_{t-1}^{2}V_{t-1}^{-1}), where M=⌈1−log⁡(K)log⁡(1−1/(4​e​π))⌉M=\lceil 1-\frac{\log(K)}{\log(1-1/(4\sqrt{e\pi}))}\rceil and αt−1\alpha_{t-1} is a confidence radius defined as

Comparison with previous works.

Closely related works in queueing bandits literature include Krishnasamy et al. (2016); Kim and Oh (2024); Bae et al. (2026). First, Krishnasamy et al. (2016) pioneered the analysis of queue length regret. However, their multi-armed bandit (MAB)-based framework ignores query contexts and assumes fixed departure rates, making it unsuitable for our setting. Second, Kim and Oh (2024) address context but restrict it to a single fixed type per queue, unlike our arbitrary setting, and they lack an analysis of queue length regret. The most comparable study is Algorithm 1 of Bae et al. (2026), which accommodates arbitrary contexts and analyzes queue length regret. Notably, it yields a tighter leading term of 𝒪(d3/2T−1/4log3/2(T)σ0−5ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(d^{3/2}T^{-1/4}\log^{3/2}(T)\sigma_{0}^{-5}\epsilon^{-3}) compared to the 𝒪(d5T−1/4log5(T)σ0−9ϵ−5)\mathcal{O}(d^{5}T^{-1/4}\log^{5}(T)\sigma_{0}^{-9}\epsilon^{-5}) term of our Algorithm 1. However, their approach relies on an exploration schedule dependent on the horizon TT and slackness ϵ\epsilon, which fails to satisfy the anytime property, making it unsuitable for continuous LLM serving (see Remark 15). Finally, their model considers only the logistic function, requiring non-trivial extension to the MNL model.

4 Regret Analysis

In this section, we provide a proof sketch for Theorems 5 and 6. The full proofs are deferred to Appendix D.

4.1 Proof Sketch of Theorem 5

Queue state misalignment.

We start by addressing queue state misalignment, a phenomenon unique to contextual queueing bandits with arbitrary contexts. To analyze the queue length difference Q​(t)−Q∗​(t)Q(t)-Q^{*}(t), we need to upper bound the expected departure rate gap 𝔼⁡[D∗​(i)−D⁡(i)]\mathbb{E}[D^{*}(i)-D(i)] for each round i<ti<t. If the queue states (i.e., the sets of pending queries) were identical under both policies at round ii, we could control this gap following an optimistic rule from the standard bandit techniques—specifically, by selecting the query-assortment pair with the highest optimistic estimate of the departure rate (as in Line 7 of Algorithm 1). However, a suboptimal decision at round ii affects the queue state for the subsequent round. Consequently, the queue state at round i+1i+1 under our policy diverges from that under the optimal policy. We call this phenomenon queue state misalignment. This misalignment invalidates standard bandit analysis because following the optimistic rule over the current queue does not guarantee optimism; the optimal policy’s queue may contain a superior query that is currently unavailable to the learner.

Coupling process, and policy switching queues.

To address such misalignment, we employ a coupling argument and define policy switching queues. We construct a collection of tt coupled queueing processes {Qi}i=0t−1\{Q_{i}\}_{i=0}^{t-1}, where each process QiQ_{i} follows our policy π\pi up to round ii and then switches to the optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} from rounds i+1i+1 to t−1t-1. Denote the corresponding queue lengths by {Q⁡(i,t)}i=0t−1\{Q(i,t)\}_{i=0}^{t-1}. These tt processes are coupled through shared randomness. Specifically, all processes experience identical query arrivals. Furthermore, if the same query and the LLM assortment are selected across processes at any given round, the realized feedback (i.e., departure or retrial) is identical. A formal definition is provided in Section D.1.

Queue length regret decomposition.

Utilizing the coupling construction, we decompose the queue length regret via the following telescoping sum:

Consequently, unlike the queue length regret analysis, this definition allows us to avoid queue state misalignment, allowing us to employ standard bandit analysis techniques.

At each round ii, the agent performs random exploration with probability η⁡(i−1)\eta(i-1) (indicated by E⁡(i−1)=1E(i-1)=1) and otherwise follows the Thompson sampling-based optimistic rule (with probability 1−η⁡(i−1)1-\eta(i-1)). Combining these two components, we obtain an overall cumulative regret bound of 𝒪~​(d3/2​t)\mathchoice{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,\left(d^{3/2}\sqrt{t}\right)}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(d^{3/2}\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(d^{3/2}\sqrt{t})}{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\,(d^{3/2}\sqrt{t})}. A detailed proof is provided in Section D.8.

5 Algorithmic Extensions

We introduce two algorithmic adaptations designed to address the challenges of real-world deployment and to enhance performance.

5.1 Capturing LLM Heterogeneity via Disjoint Parameterization

Many prior works (Chiang et al., 2025; Shirkavand et al., 2025a) adopt a formulation that uses joint feature vector xt,jx_{t,j}—combining characteristics from the query xtx_{t} and the LLM jj—along with a shared parameter vector θ∗\theta^{*}. However, implementing this in practice presents significant challenges. While obtaining a representation for the query xtx_{t} is straightforward using pre-trained query embedding models (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Sentence-Transformers, 2021), constructing the joint feature xt,jx_{t,j} (i.e., fusing LLM jj’s characteristics into xtx_{t}) remains a heuristic and inconsistent process across different studies. This heavy reliance on feature engineering obfuscates the true source of improvements, making it difficult to distinguish whether performance gains stem from the routing algorithm itself or merely from sophisticated feature construction.

Therefore, for the experiments, we adopt a disjoint parameter model to bypass the reliance on manual feature engineering. In this setting, the query context xtx_{t} is shared, but each server jj is governed by a unique unknown parameter θj∗\theta_{j}^{*}. This allows the agent to learn the unique characteristics of heterogeneous LLMs through online learning, thereby removing the confounding effects of feature engineering and enabling a fair assessment of algorithmic performance. Accordingly, define the collection of parameters as Θ∗=[θ1∗,θ2∗,…,θN∗]∈ℝd×N\Theta^{*}=[\theta_{1}^{*},\theta_{2}^{*},\dots,\theta_{N}^{*}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}. When a user with context xx is presented with an assortment SS, the probability pj​(x,S,Θ∗)p_{j}(x,S,\Theta^{*}) of selecting item jj and the corresponding departure rate R⁡(x,S,Θ∗)R(x,S,\Theta^{*}) are defined as pj​(x,S,Θ∗):=exp⁡(x⊤​θj∗)1+∑j′∈Sexp⁡(x⊤​θj′∗)p_{j}(x,S,\Theta^{*}):=\frac{\exp(x^{\top}\theta_{j}^{*})}{1+\sum_{j^{\prime}\in S}\exp(x^{\top}\theta_{j^{\prime}}^{*})} for j∈Sj\in S, p0​(x,S,Θ∗):=11+∑j′∈Sexp⁡(x⊤​θj′∗)p_{0}(x,S,\Theta^{*}):=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j^{\prime}\in S}\exp(x^{\top}\theta_{j^{\prime}}^{*})} for j=0j=0, and R⁡(x,S,Θ∗):=∑j∈Spj​(x,S,Θ∗)R(x,S,\Theta^{*}):=\sum_{j\in S}p_{j}(x,S,\Theta^{*}). Under this disjoint model, the agent maintains separate statistics for each model jj: a design matrix Vt,jV_{t,j}, a maximum likelihood estimator θ^t,j\hat{\theta}_{t,j}, and a confidence radius αt,j\alpha_{t,j}. The detailed algorithm is outlined in Section B.1.

Remark 7.

Notice that this disjoint parameterization is a specific instance of the shared parameter setting used in our theoretical analysis. Let ej∈ℝNe_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} be the standard basis vector with a 11 at the jj-th position and 00 elsewhere. Then, for all j∈[N]j\in[N], we can write x𝖳​θj∗=(x⊗ej)𝖳​vec​(Θ∗)x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*}=(x\otimes e_{j})^{\mathsf{T}}\text{vec}(\Theta^{*}) where ⊗\otimes denotes the Kronecker product and vec​(Θ∗)\text{vec}(\Theta^{*}) represents the vectorization of a matrix. By viewing (x⊗ej)∈ℝd​N(x\otimes e_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{dN} as a feature vector and vec​(Θ∗)∈ℝd​N\text{vec}(\Theta^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{dN} as the shared parameter, our theoretical analysis remains valid.

5.2 Utility-Aligned Query Embeddings via Contrastive Learning

Standard query encoders are typically trained to align representations with linguistic semantics (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), resulting in an embedding space where proximity reflects categorical or paraphrase-level similarity (Chiang et al., 2025). However, effective multi-LLM routing requires embeddings to capture utility alignment rather than semantic closeness. That is, two queries should be considered similar if they exhibit similar routing utilities (i.e., performance-cost trade-offs) across varying LLMs, even if they are semantically distinct (Chen et al., 2024). To address this, we propose ACQB-CL (Algorithms 2 and 3), which realigns the query representation space. Specifically, given a raw prompt ξ\xi, we freeze the backbone encoder E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot) and train a two-layer MLP projection head B⁡(⋅,θ)B(\cdot;\theta) to obtain a utility-aligned representation z=B⁡(E⁡(ξ),θ)∈ℝd′z=B(E(\xi);\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}} The projection head is optimized via an InfoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018) on an offline dataset to cluster queries with similar utilities while separating divergent ones. Comprehensive details regarding offline data construction, pair selection, and the precise loss formulation are provided in Section B.2.

6 Experiments

In this section, we empirically evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithms.

6.1 Experiments on Synthetic Data

We generate random instances for K={1,2}K=\{1,2\} by setting the arrival rates to λ=0.7\lambda=0.7 with the parameters d=5d=5, ϵ=0.03\epsilon=0.03, N=5N=5, and T=1,000T=1{,}000. The context vectors x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and disjoint parameters θj∗∈ℝd\theta_{j}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for j∈[N]j\in[N] are sampled from Unif⁡(−1,1)\Unif(-1,1), ensuring that the contexts satisfy the slackness condition, i.e., maxS∈𝒞⁡R⁡(x,S,Θ∗)≥λ+ϵ\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\Theta^{*})\geq\lambda+\epsilon. We perform 10 independent runs and report the average queue length regret and average cumulative regret with ±1\pm 1 standard deviation. We benchmark ACQB against five baseline algorithms for K=1K=1: (i) the Optimal policy; (ii) the Random policy, which selects a random query and assortment; (iii–iv) two MAB-based queueing bandit algorithms from (Krishnasamy et al., 2021); and (v) the contextual queueing bandit algorithm (Algorithm 1 from Bae et al. (2026)). To the best of our knowledge, aside from these queueing bandit-based approaches, no other existing baselines are capable of learning from user retrials (implicit feedback). For the K=2K=2 setting, since baselines (iii) and (iv) are incompatible with the MNL model, we compare ACQB only with (i), (ii), and the MNL-adapted version of (v). Detailed descriptions of each baseline policy are provided in Section B.3. As shown in Figure 2, ACQB consistently outperforms baselines in both queue length and cumulative regrets. Additional experiments with varying NN and ϵ\epsilon are available in Section C.1.

6.2 Experiments on Real-World Data

For the real-world evaluation, we additionally include ACQB-CL in our comparison across three datasets: SPROUT-o3mini (14 LLMs) (Somerstep et al., 2025), EmbedLLM (112 LLMs) (Zhuang et al., 2024), and RouterBench (11 LLMs) (Hu et al., 2024). All datasets include benchmark-specific correctness scores (e.g., exact-match or graded accuracy) and inference costs. For RouterBench, we use the provided cost metadata, while for EmbedLLM and SPROUT-o3mini, we construct the cost map using reports from (Shirkavand et al., 2025b; Somerstep et al., 2025). For the query embedding, we adopt the sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2  (Sentence-Transformers, 2021) as the backbone query encoder (d=384d=384). In the online phase, we run the contextual bandit simulation over an online prompt pool of size 1,000 for a horizon of T=5,000T=5{,}000.

Modeling departure and choice probabilities.

For every LLM jj and raw prompt ξ\xi, we denote the provided performance score and normalized inference cost as perfj​(ξ)∈[0,1]\mathrm{perf}_{j}(\xi)\in[0,1] and costj​(ξ)∈[0,1]\mathrm{cost}_{j}(\xi)\in[0,1], respectively. We interpret perfj​(ξ)\mathrm{perf}_{j}(\xi) as the probability that model jj produces an acceptable response. For example, a binary score implies an outcome in {0,1}\{0,1\}, whereas a graded accuracy like 0.80.8 represents an expected acceptance probability of 0.80.8. Accordingly, we define a job to depart the queue exactly when the served response is accepted. To incorporate cost-efficiency, we define the cost-penalized routing utility as uj​(ξ)=perfj​(ξ)−ρ⋅costj​(ξ)u_{j}(\xi)=\mathrm{perf}_{j}(\xi)-\rho\cdot\mathrm{cost}_{j}(\xi). Letting x=E⁡(ξ)x=E(\xi), we model the departure probability for model jj directly as uj​(ξ)u_{j}(\xi). Under this formulation, the induced choice probability over an assortment SS is given by p⁡(j∣x,S)=uj​(1−uj)−11+∑k∈Suk​(1−uk)−1p(j\mid x,S)=\frac{u_{j}(1-u_{j})^{-1}}{1+\sum_{k\in S}u_{k}(1-u_{k})^{-1}}. The detailed derivation is provided in Section B.4.

Performance comparison.

We benchmark ACQB and ACQB-CL against baseline algorithms under varying load conditions. Specifically, we set the arrival rates to λ∈{0.7,0.8,0.9}\lambda\in\{0.7,0.8,0.9\} for assortment size K=1K=1 and λ∈{0.75,0.85,0.95}\lambda\in\{0.75,0.85,0.95\} for K=2K=2. Figure 3 illustrates the queue length and cumulative regrets on the SPROUT-o3mini dataset. In terms of queue stability, baseline algorithms often suffer from rapid queue growth under high arrival rates, indicating a failure to stabilize the system. In contrast, ACQB and ACQB-CL maintain substantially lower and more stable queue lengths, with ACQB-CL demonstrating superior stability. Both algorithms outperform all baselines in cumulative regret, exhibiting sublinear growth across all configurations. Notably, ACQB-CL consistently achieves lower cumulative regret than ACQB, confirming the benefit of contrastive learning. Additional results on other datasets are provided in Section C.2.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce a novel online learning framework, contextual queueing bandits with MNL feedback (CQB-MNL), for joint LLM routing and scheduling. This framework is specifically designed for practical settings where user dissatisfaction triggers retrials and explicit feedback is unavailable. We propose anytime CQB (ACQB), which guarantees both a sublinear cumulative regret and a decaying queue length regret bound. By leveraging time-decaying exploration probability, ACQB avoids dependence on time horizon or traffic slackness parameter, balancing sufficient learning while maintaining queue stability. Finally, we further enhance practicality via disjoint parameterization and query embedding refinement using contrastive learning (ACQB-CL), as validated by our experiments.

Appendix A Related Work

LLM routing and scheduling.

LLM routing selects models to balance quality and cost, while LLM scheduling determines the service order of pending requests to minimize latency. Although substantial research has relied on supervised learning with offline datasets, such as Ong et al. (2024); Feng et al. (2024); Lu et al. (2024); Somerstep et al. (2025) for routing and Fu et al. (2024); Shahout et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2025) for scheduling, recent works have emerged that utilize online learning to address the high costs of offline annotation and the non-stationarity of real-world environments (Mohammadshahi et al., 2024; Wu and Silwal, 2025; Chiang et al., 2025; Jitkrittum et al., 2025; Jaillet et al., 2025; Ao et al., 2025). However, these methods neglect the interactive nature of LLMs, either ignoring congestion caused by retrials or disrupting user experience by requiring explicit feedback.

Queueing bandits.

The queueing bandit framework, originally designed to address routing problems in systems with unknown service rates, was introduced by Krishnasamy et al. (2016). This seminal work has inspired a significant body of research establishing queue stability—ensuring that expected queue lengths remain bounded—and deriving queue length regret bounds across various settings (Liang and Modiano, 2018; Stahlbuhk et al., 2021; Choudhury et al., 2021; Krishnasamy et al., 2021; Wijewardena et al., 2025). More recently, this framework has been extended to the contextual setting, incorporating job-specific features and adopting logistic models for departure dynamics (Kim and Oh, 2024; Bae et al., 2026). However, the approach of Kim and Oh (2024) is limited by a fixed context assumption. While Bae et al. (2026) accommodate heterogeneous contexts, their reliance on the time horizon and traffic slackness parameter hinders practical deployment.

Logistic Bandits.

Starting with the seminal work on generalized linear bandits (Filippi et al., 2010), the (multinomial) logistic bandit problem has been extensively studied due to its effectiveness in modeling discrete user choices and categorical feedback (Li et al., 2017; Agrawal et al., 2019; Oh and Iyengar, 2019; Jun et al., 2021; Abeille et al., 2021; Bae and Lee, 2025; Lee and Oh, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). In this work, we adopt the MNL model for queue dynamics (Kim and Oh, 2024; Bae et al., 2026) and directly apply these analytical tools to bound the departure rate gap between the optimal policy and our proposed policy.

B.2 Utility-Aligned Query Embeddings via Contrastive Learning

This section details the utility-based contrastive learning framework for ACQB-CL, extending the overview in Section 5.2. The goal of this offline phase is to train the projection head B⁡(⋅,θ)B(\cdot;\theta) appended to the frozen encoder E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot). Leveraging an offline dataset containing utility values (i.e., performance and cost) for all servers, we aim to structure the embedding space such that queries with similar routing utilities are clustered together, while those with dissimilar utilities are separated.

We begin the process by constructing a balanced offline dataset from the representation learning split. Specifically, we employ a model-balanced sampling strategy. For each available prompt ξ\xi, we compute the utility vector {uj​(ξ)}j=1N\{u_{j}(\xi)\}_{j=1}^{N} across all models and identify the optimal model that yields the highest utility. We then group prompts according to their optimal model index. To ensure diversity, we uniformly sample a fixed number of prompts (e.g., 5 prompts in our experiments for Sprout data) from each group. This procedure ensures that the offline training set is composed of samples selected evenly across all candidate LLMs.

Offline Training Algorithm.

After sampling, we form the offline dataset as 𝒟off={(ξ(i),u(i))}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}}=\{(\xi_{(i)},u_{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}, where ξ(i)\xi_{(i)} denotes the selected prompt and u(i)u_{(i)} represents its utility vector across all models. We use the frozen encoder outputs x(i)=E⁡(ξ(i))x_{(i)}=E(\xi_{(i)}) and the utility vectors u(i)u_{(i)} to train the two-layer MLP projection head B⁡(⋅,θ)B(\cdot;\theta). Algorithm 3 summarizes the procedure.

At the beginning of each epoch, we compute the projected representation z(i)=B⁡(x(i),θ)z_{(i)}=B(x_{(i)};\theta) for each offline prompt. To determine similarity targets, we first mean-center each utility vector across models:

u¯(i)←u(i)−mean⁡(u(i)).\bar{u}_{(i)}\leftarrow u_{(i)}-\mathrm{mean}(u_{(i)}).

We then compute the pairwise utility similarity c(i,j)c_{(i,j)} for all i≠ji\neq j using the cosine similarity of these centered vectors:

c(i,j)←cos⁡(u¯(i),u¯(j)):=u¯(i)⊤​u¯(j)‖u¯(i)‖2​‖u¯(j)‖2.c_{(i,j)}\leftarrow\cos(\bar{u}_{(i)},\bar{u}_{(j)}):=\frac{\bar{u}_{(i)}^{\top}\bar{u}_{(j)}}{\|\bar{u}_{(i)}\|_{2}\,\|\bar{u}_{(j)}\|_{2}}.

This metric is used for selecting positive and negative pairs. Given a pair of thresholds (ιpos,ιneg)(\iota_{\mathrm{pos}},\iota_{\mathrm{neg}}), we define the candidate positive set P⁡(i)P(i) and negative set N⁡(i)N(i) as

P⁡(i)={j≠i:c(i,j)>ιpos},N⁡(i)={j≠i:c(i,j)<ιneg}.P(i)=\{j\neq i:\ c_{(i,j)}>\iota_{\mathrm{pos}}\},\quad N(i)=\{j\neq i:\ c_{(i,j)}<\iota_{\mathrm{neg}}\}.

Any candidate jj with similarity falling between the thresholds (i.e., ιneg≤c(i,j)≤ιpos\iota_{\mathrm{neg}}\leq c_{(i,j)}\leq\iota_{\mathrm{pos}}) is ignored. From the positive set P⁡(i)P(i), we select the single best positive example j+j^{+} that maximizes utility similarity, i.e. j+∈arg⁡maxj∈P⁡(i)⁡c(i,j)j^{+}\in\arg\max_{j\in P(i)}c_{(i,j)}. For the negative set, we construct a subset 𝒩(i)⊆N⁡(i)\mathcal{N}_{(i)}\subseteq N(i) to limit computational cost. Specifically, we select up to KnegK_{\mathrm{neg}} hard negatives (those with the smallest similarity values c(i,j)c_{(i,j)}). If P⁡(i)P(i) is empty or no negatives remain, we skip the update for query ii.

Using the selected positive j+j^{+} and negative set 𝒩(i)\mathcal{N}_{(i)}, we compute the representation similarity sim⁡(z(i),z(j))=z(i)⊤​z(j)\mathrm{sim}(z_{(i)},z_{(j)})=z_{(i)}^{\top}z_{(j)} and define the InfoNCE loss with temperature τtemp\tau_{\mathrm{temp}} as

ℓ(i)​(θ)=−log⁡exp⁡(sim⁡(z(i),z(j+))/τtemp)exp⁡(sim⁡(z(i),z(j+))/τtemp)+∑j∈𝒩(i)exp⁡(sim⁡(z(i),z(j))/τtemp).\displaystyle\ell_{(i)}(\theta)=-\log\dfrac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_{(i)},z_{(j^{+})})/\tau_{\mathrm{temp}})}{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_{(i)},z_{(j^{+})})/\tau_{\mathrm{temp}})+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{(i)}}\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_{(i)},z_{(j)})/\tau_{\mathrm{temp}})}. (5)

Finally, we update the projection head parameters θ\theta via gradient descent over all valid queries:

θ←θ−η∇θ∑i:|P⁡(i)|>0ℓ(i)(θ).\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_{\theta}\sum_{i:\,|P(i)|>0}\ell_{(i)}(\theta).

After offline pretraining, we freeze the projection head B⁡(⋅,θ)B(\cdot;\theta) and proceed to the online learning stage described in Algorithm 2.

Experimental Settings.

We use τtemp=0.07\tau_{\mathrm{temp}}=0.07 and a negative cap Kneg=64K_{\mathrm{neg}}=64. The projection head is a two-layer MLP with an output dimension of 384384, matching the encoder dimension. We set distinct threshold pairs (ιpos,ιneg)(\iota_{\mathrm{pos}},\iota_{\mathrm{neg}}) for each dataset: (0.6,0.3)(0.6,0.3) for SPROUT-o3mini, (0.4,0.1)(0.4,0.1) for EmbedLLM, and (0.5,0.3)(0.5,0.3) for RouterBench. For contrastive pretraining of BB in an offline setting, we use 5 prompts per model for SPROUT-o3mini and train for 10 epochs; for EmbedLLM, we use 10 prompts per model (30 prompts per epoch) and train for 50 epochs.

B.3 Baseline Algorithms

We compare our proposed ACQB and ACQB-CL algorithms against the following baselines:

  1. (i)

    Optimal Policy: The optimal policy has full access to the true set of disjoint parameters Θ∗={θj∗}j=1N\Theta^{*}=\{\theta_{j}^{*}\}_{j=1}^{N}. In every round tt, given the set of backlogged queries 𝒳t∗\mathcal{X}_{t}^{*}, it selects the query-assortment pair (x∗,S∗)(x^{*},S^{*}) that maximizes the expected departure rate:

    (x∗,S∗)∈arg​maxx∈𝒳t∗,S∈𝒞⁡R​(x,S,Θ∗).\displaystyle(x^{*},S^{*})\in\argmax_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{*},S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\Theta^{*}).
  2. (ii)

    Random Policy: In every round tt, the random policy selects a query xtx_{t} uniformly at random from the current backlog and chooses an assortment StS_{t} uniformly at random from the feasible set 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

  3. (iii)

    Q-UCB (Krishnasamy et al., 2021, Algorithm 1): This is a MAB-based algorithm designed for the single-item setting (K=1K=1). Since this algorithm treats all queries as identical ignoring their contexts, it employs a first-in-first-out (FIFO) scheduling rule, simply selecting the oldest job in the queue as xtx_{t}. The algorithm explores with probability min⁡{1,3​N​(log2⁡t)/t}\min\{1,3N(\log^{2}t)/t\}. For the assortment selection, it chooses the item that maximizes the upper confidence bound (UCB):

    St=arg​maxS∈𝒞,|S|=1⁡(μ^S​(t)+log2⁡t2​TS​(t−1)),\displaystyle S_{t}=\argmax_{S\in\mathcal{C},|S|=1}\left(\widehat{\mu}_{S}(t)+\sqrt{\frac{\log^{2}t}{2T_{S}(t-1)}}\right),

    where μ^S(t)=∑i=1t−1𝟏{Si=S}yi/TS(t−1)\widehat{\mu}_{S}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbf{1}\,\mathchoice{\left\{S_{i}=S\right\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}y_{i}/T_{S}(t-1) is the empirical mean reward and TS(t−1)=∑i=1t−1𝟏{Si=S}T_{S}(t-1)=\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbf{1}\,\mathchoice{\left\{S_{i}=S\right\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}{\{S_{i}=S\}}is the number of times assortment SS has been played up to time t−1t-1.

  4. (iv)

    Q-ThS (Krishnasamy et al., 2021, Algorithm 2): Similar to Q-UCB, this is an MAB-based approach for K=1K=1 using FIFO scheduling. It explores with the same probability schedule as Q-UCB. For every assortment selection StS_{t}, it samples a departure rate estimate from a Beta posterior:

    r~t​(xt,S)∼Beta​(μ^S​(t)​TS​(t−1)+1,(1−μ^S​(t))​TS​(t−1)+1).\displaystyle\widetilde{r}_{t}(x_{t},S)\sim\text{Beta}\Big(\widehat{\mu}_{S}(t)T_{S}(t-1)+1,(1-\widehat{\mu}_{S}(t))T_{S}(t-1)+1\Big).

    It then selects the assortment StS_{t} that maximizes this sampled value, i.e. St:=arg​maxK=1,S∈𝒞⁡r~t​(xt,S)S_{t}:=\argmax_{K=1,S\in\mathcal{C}}\widetilde{r}_{t}(x_{t},S), where we use the same definitions of μ^S​(t)\widehat{\mu}_{S}(t) and TS​(t−1)T_{S}(t-1) as Q-UCB.

  5. (v)

    CQB-ε\bm{\varepsilon} (Adapted from Bae et al. (2026)): This baseline is an adaptation of the contextual queueing bandit algorithm from Bae et al. (2026). While the original algorithm was developed as a UCB-based approach under logistic feedback, we modified it to utilize Thompson Sampling with MNL feedback. This adaptation ensures a fair and consistent comparison with our proposed framework under the same environmental assumptions.

    Let τ\tau denote the length of the pure-exploration phase. If A⁡(t−1)=1A(t-1)=1 and the agent is either in the exploration phase (t≤τt\leq\tau) or triggers a random exploration with probability T−1/2T^{-1/2}, it selects xt←x(t−1)x_{t}\leftarrow x^{(t-1)} (the most recent job) and chooses StS_{t} in a round-robin manner. Otherwise, it follows the optimistic rule described in ACQB (Line 6–9 of Algorithm 2).

    Notice that the theoretical requirement for the exploration length of CQB-𝜺\bm{\varepsilon}, τ=𝒪⁡(d​log⁡(T)σ04​ϵ2)\tau=\mathcal{O}(\frac{d\log(T)}{\sigma_{0}^{4}\epsilon^{2}}), is often prohibitively large for practical experiments. Therefore, we adopt distinct practical heuristics depending on the experimental setting. For synthetic data experiments, following previous work (Bae et al., 2026), we set a fixed exploration length of τ=T/10\tau=T/10. For real-world datasets, we determine τ\tau by aligning it with the stabilization point of our exploration rate η⁡(t)\eta(t). Specifically, we set τ=min{t:c1(t+1)−1/2≤1}\tau=\min\{t:c_{1}(t+1)^{-1/2}\leq 1\}, ensuring that the pure-exploration phase ends when ACQB’s exploration probability drops below 1.

B.4 Modeling Departure and Choice Probabilities for Real-World Experiment

This section details how we transform raw utility scores into departure and choice probabilities, complementing the experimental setup in Section 6.2. Recall that for a raw prompt ξ\xi and model jj, we define the (raw) utility as ujraw​(ξ)=perfj​(ξ)−ρ⋅costj​(ξ)u_{j}^{\text{raw}}(\xi)=\mathrm{perf}_{j}(\xi)-\rho\cdot\mathrm{cost}_{j}(\xi). Since this value may fall outside the feasible probability range [0,1][0,1] depending on ρ\rho, we apply a two-step transformation. First, we apply min-max normalization over the models to obtain a value in [0,1][0,1]:

ujnorm​(ξ)=ujraw​(ξ)−mink⁡ukraw​(ξ)maxk⁡ukraw​(ξ)−mink⁡ukraw​(ξ).\displaystyle u_{j}^{\text{norm}}(\xi)=\frac{u_{j}^{\text{raw}}(\xi)-\min_{k}u_{k}^{\text{raw}}(\xi)}{\max_{k}u_{k}^{\text{raw}}(\xi)-\min_{k}u_{k}^{\text{raw}}(\xi)}.

Next, to prevent extreme probabilities (0 or 1) that can cause numerical instability, we linearly rescale this normalized value to a bounded range [rlo,rhi]⊆[0,1][r_{\mathrm{lo}},r_{\mathrm{hi}}]\subseteq[0,1]. We define the final departure probability uj​(ξ)u_{j}(\xi) as:

uj​(ξ):=rlo+(rhi−rlo)⋅ujnorm​(ξ),\displaystyle u_{j}(\xi):=r_{\mathrm{lo}}+(r_{\mathrm{hi}}-r_{\mathrm{lo}})\cdot u_{j}^{\text{norm}}(\xi),

where we set rlo=0.1r_{\mathrm{lo}}=0.1 and rhi=0.99r_{\mathrm{hi}}=0.99 in our experiments.

We define the true departure probability for prompt ξ\xi on model jj as this transformed value uj​(ξ)u_{j}(\xi). To consistent with our MNL choice framework, let x=E⁡(ξ)x=E(\xi) denote the query context. We construct the latent reward x𝖳​θj∗x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*} such that its logistic function matches the departure probability:

uj​(ξ)=exp⁡(x𝖳​θj∗)1+exp⁡(x𝖳​θj∗)⟹exp⁡(x𝖳​θj∗)=uj​(ξ)1−uj​(ξ).\displaystyle u_{j}(\xi)=\frac{\exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*})}{1+\exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*})}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*})=\frac{u_{j}(\xi)}{1-u_{j}(\xi)}.

Substituting this relationship into the MNL choice model for an assortment SS, we derive the final choice probabilities entirely in terms of the derived utilities:

p⁡(j∣x,S)=exp⁡(x𝖳​θj∗)1+∑k∈Sexp⁡(x𝖳​θk∗)=uj​(ξ)1−uj​(ξ)1+∑k∈Suk​(ξ)1−uk​(ξ).\displaystyle p(j\mid x,S)=\frac{\exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{j}^{*})}{1+\sum_{k\in S}\exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}\theta_{k}^{*})}=\frac{\frac{u_{j}(\xi)}{1-u_{j}(\xi)}}{1+\sum_{k\in S}\frac{u_{k}(\xi)}{1-u_{k}(\xi)}}.

D.2 Queue Length Regret Decomposition

Now we focus on this quantity ψ⁡(i,t):=Q⁡(i,t)−Q⁡(i−1,t)\psi(i,t):=Q(i,t)-Q(i-1,t). As the two coupled queues follow the same randomness and the same policy up to round t−1t-1, their queue states at time step tt are identical. With this alignment, the following lemma characterize ψ⁡(i,t)\psi(i,t):

Lemma 8.

We have ψ⁡(i,t)∈{−1,0,1}\psi(i,t)\in\{-1,0,1\} for all i∈[0,t−1]i\in[0,t-1]. Moreover, the expected value of ψ⁡(i,t)\psi(i,t) can be decomposed even further as follows:

Lemma 9.

ℱl+\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{l}^{+} :=ℱl∨σ⁡(E⁡(l−1),𝑨⁡(l),𝜽⁡(l)),\displaystyle:=\mathcal{F}_{l}\lor\sigma(E(l-1),\bm{A}(l),\bm{\theta}(l)),

Bad rounds.

We can see that x~l\widetilde{x}_{l} and S~l\widetilde{S}_{l} are both ℱl\mathcal{F}_{l}-measurable since ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is only short for E⁡(t−1)E(t-1), therefore 𝒳t\mathcal{X}_{t} and {θ~t−1(i)}i=1M\{\widetilde{\theta}_{t-1}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{M} is still ℱl\mathcal{F}_{l}-measurable, which include sufficient information to compute x~l\widetilde{x}_{l} and S~l\widetilde{S}_{l}. Next, we introduce the formal definition of bad rounds and good rounds: We denote all rounds up to τ⁡(t)\tau(t) as bad rounds and τ⁡(t)+1\tau(t)+1 to tt as good rounds. Define the set of bad rounds as ℬ\mathcal{B}. Then by the direct result of Proposition 14, on the event ℰg\mathcal{E}_{g} and ℰ0​(l)c\mathcal{E}_{0}(l)^{c}, for all l∉ℬl\notin\mathcal{B}, we have

Remark 15.

Bae et al. (2026) also derive a departure rate gap bound of ϵ/2−η\epsilon/2-\eta similar to Equation 8, where η=T−1/2\eta=T^{-1/2}. Their method, however, necessitates a pure-exploration phase at the beginning, calculating the required exploration amount based on the horizon TT and slackness ϵ\epsilon. In contrast, we employ a time-varying exploration rate η⁡(t)\eta(t) to bypass this dependence. We show that setting the threshold τ⁡(t)\tau(t) as defined in Equation 7 ensures that the accumulated random exploration is sufficient to satisfy the departure rate upper bound in Equation 8, thereby achieving an anytime guarantee without prior knowledge.

Next, we establish that for good rounds there is a negative drift as described in the following lemma:

Lemma 16.

On the event ℰg\mathcal{E}_{g}, for all l∉ℬl\notin\mathcal{B}, i∈[0,t−1]i\in[0,t-1], we have

𝔼[A(l)−D(i,l)∣ℱl]≤−ϵ/2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[A(l)-D(i,l)\mid\mathcal{F}_{l}]\leq-\epsilon/2.

In this paragraph, we give the upper bound for the expected queue length difference between two consecutive policy-switching queues, which is ψ⁡(i,t)\psi(i,t). Consider i∈[0,t−1]i\in[0,t-1]. We first specify the conditions on tt required for Theorem 5.

Appendix E Deferred Proofs for Section D.2

E.1 Proof of Lemma 8

To characterize ψ⁡(t,T)=Q⁡(i,t)−Q⁡(i−1,t)\psi(t,T)=Q(i,t)-Q(i-1,t), we understand the dynamics of the coupled queues of QiQ_{i} and Qi−1Q_{i-1}. Notice that in l∈[i+1,t]l\in[i+1,t], both QiQ_{i} and Qi−1Q_{i-1} follows the same optimal policy. Therefore, to track down the queue length difference, we don’t need to consider about the context of the job inside the queue xx itself; instead, we only need to consider the optimal departure rate of the corresponding job maxS∈𝒞⁡R⁡(x,S,θ∗)\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*}). For example, if there are two different job but with the same departure rate, i.e. for x1≠x2x_{1}\neq x_{2} and maxS∈𝒞⁡R⁡(x1,S,θ∗)=maxS∈𝒞⁡R⁡(x2,S,θ∗)\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x_{1},S,\theta^{*})=\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x_{2},S,\theta^{*}), we don’t have to distinguish whether the optimal policy choose x1x_{1} or x2x_{2} since the optimal policy does not involve the learning procedure and the queue length will evolve same by the coupling process. Accordingly, we introduce the new definitions: Define 𝒳⁡(i,t′)\mathcal{X}(i,t^{\prime}) for the queue state of QiQ_{i} in round t′t^{\prime}. Then we define the departure rate set of the queue state as

𝒟(i,t′):={d(x),∀x∈𝒳(i,t′):d(x)=maxS∈𝒞R(x,S,θ∗)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(i,t^{\prime}):=\mathchoice{\left\{d(x),~\forall x\in\mathcal{X}(i,t^{\prime}):~d(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*})\right\}}{\{d(x),~\forall x\in\mathcal{X}(i,t^{\prime}):~d(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*})\}}{\{d(x),~\forall x\in\mathcal{X}(i,t^{\prime}):~d(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*})\}}{\{d(x),~\forall x\in\mathcal{X}(i,t^{\prime}):~d(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{C}}R(x,S,\theta^{*})\}}.

For l∈[i+1,t]l\in[i+1,t], let us consider the following five states:

Sl,0\displaystyle S_{l,0} ={𝒟(i,l)=𝒟(i−1,l)}\displaystyle=\{\mathcal{D}(i,l)=\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\}
Sl,1\displaystyle S_{l,1} ={𝒟(i,l)∖𝒟(i−1,l)={dl+},𝒟(i,l)⊃𝒟(i−1,l)}\displaystyle=\{\mathcal{D}(i,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)=\{d_{l}^{+}\},~\mathcal{D}(i,l)\supset\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\}
Sl,2\displaystyle S_{l,2} ={𝒟(i−1,l)∖𝒟(i,l)={dl−},𝒟(i−1,l)⊃𝒟(i,l)}\displaystyle=\{\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i,l)=\{d_{l}^{-}\},~\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\supset\mathcal{D}(i,l)\}
Sl,3\displaystyle S_{l,3} ={𝒟(i,l)∖𝒟(i−1,l)={dl+},𝒟(i−1,l)∖𝒟(i,l)={dl−},dl+>dl−}\displaystyle=\{\mathcal{D}(i,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)=\{d_{l}^{+}\},~\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i,l)=\{d_{l}^{-}\},~d_{l}^{+}>d_{l}^{-}\}
Sl,4\displaystyle S_{l,4} ={𝒟(i,l)∖𝒟(i−1,l)={dl+},𝒟(i−1,l)∖𝒟(i,l)={dl−},dl+<dl−}.\displaystyle=\{\mathcal{D}(i,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)=\{d_{l}^{+}\},~\mathcal{D}(i-1,l)\setminus\mathcal{D}(i,l)=\{d_{l}^{-}\},~d_{l}^{+}<d_{l}^{-}\}.

Now we proceed with the proof as follows:

  1. 1.

    We show that under optimal policy, Sl,s′S_{l,s^{\prime}} only transits to Sl+1,s′′S_{l+1,s^{\prime\prime}} where s′,s′′∈{0,1,2,3,4}s^{\prime},s^{\prime\prime}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}.

  2. 2.

    We show that in round i+1i+1, the state is inside Sl,s′S_{l,s^{\prime}}, thereby at the end of round tt, it will still resides inside those five states, which implies ψ⁡(i,t)∈{−1,0,1}\psi(i,t)\in\{-1,0,1\}.

First, we consider each case Sl,s′S_{l,s^{\prime}} for s′∈{0,1,2,3,4}s^{\prime}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}

  1. (case 1)

    If round ll is in state Sl,0S_{l,0}, then 𝒟⁡(i,l)=𝒟⁡(i−1,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l)=\mathcal{D}(i-1,l), so the optimal policy would choose the same job. As a result, round l+1l+1 would be in state Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0}.

  2. (case 2)

    If round ll is in state Sl,1S_{l,1}, it falls into the following two cases, based on whether the optimal policy chooses dl+d_{l}^{+} for 𝒟⁡(i,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l).

    1. (case 2-1)

      If the optimal policy selects di+d_{i}^{+} for 𝒟⁡(i,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l), this means that D⁡(i,i)≥D⁡(i−1,i)D(i,i)\geq D(i-1,i). Therefore, there are three possibilities. When D⁡(i,i)=D⁡(i,i)=0D(i,i)=D(i,i)=0, as the queues keep the same sets of for round l+1l+1, we have Sl+1,1S_{l+1,1} for round l+1l+1. If D⁡(i,i)=D⁡(i,i−1)=1D(i,i)=D(i,i-1)=1, as the optimal policy would choose another job in 𝒟⁡(i,i−1)\mathcal{D}(i,i-1), we still have state Sl+1,1S_{l+1,1} for round l+1l+1. When D⁡(i,i)=1D(i,i)=1 and D⁡(i,i−1)=0D(i,i-1)=0, round i+1i+1 would be in state Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0}.

    2. (case 2-2)

  3. (case 3)

    If round ll is in state Sl,2S_{l,2}, by the symmetry between Sl,1S_{l,1} and Sl,2S_{l,2}, we can argue that we have Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0} or Sl+1,2S_{l+1,2} in round l+1l+1 with a similar argument as in case 2.

  4. (case 4)

    If round ll is in state Sl,4S_{l,4}, it falls into the following two cases, based on whether the optimal policy chooses dt+d_{t}^{+} for 𝒟⁡(i,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l).

    1. (case 4-1)

      If the optimal policy selects dl+d_{l}^{+} for Q⁡(i,l)Q(i,l), this means that D⁡(i,l)≥D⁡(i−1,l)D(i,l)\geq D(i-1,l). Therefore, there are three possibilities. When D⁡(i,l)=D⁡(i−1,l)=0D(i,l)=D(i-1,l)=0, as the queues keep the same sets of jobs for round l+1l+1, we have Sl+1,4S_{l+1,4} for round l+1l+1. If D⁡(i,l)=D⁡(i−1,l)=1D(i,l)=D(i-1,l)=1, the optimal policy would choose another job in 𝒟⁡(i−1,l)\mathcal{D}(i-1,l). If the optimal policy chooses dl−d_{l}^{-} from 𝒟⁡(i−1,l)\mathcal{D}(i-1,l), we have state Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0} in round l+1l+1. If not, round l+1l+1 would be in state S1,4S_{1,4}. When D⁡(i,l)=1D(i,l)=1 and D⁡(i−1,l)=0D(i-1,l)=0, round l+1l+1 would be in state Sl+1,2S_{l+1,2}.

    2. (case 4-2)

      If the optimal policy does not choose dl+d_{l}^{+} for 𝒟⁡(i,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l), then it would not choose dl−d_{l}^{-} from 𝒟⁡(i−1,l)\mathcal{D}(i-1,l) either. Hence, the optimal policy chooses the same job for 𝒟⁡(i,l)\mathcal{D}(i,l) and 𝒟⁡(i−1,l)\mathcal{D}(i-1,l), so round l+1l+1 would be in state Sl+1,3S_{l+1,3}.

    In summary, for (case 4), we have Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0} or Sl+1,2S_{l+1,2} or Sl+1,3S_{l+1,3} in round l+1l+1.

  5. (case 5)

    If round ii is in state Sl,4S_{l,4}, by the symmetry between Sl,3S_{l,3} and Sl,4S_{l,4}, we may argue that we have Sl+1,0S_{l+1,0} or Sl+1,1S_{l+1,1} or Sl+1,4S_{l+1,4} in round l+1l+1 with a similar argument as in (case 4).

The results above show that for l∈[i+1,t]l\in[i+1,t], Sl,s′S_{l,s^{\prime}} only transits to Sl+1,s′′S_{l+1,s^{\prime\prime}} where s′,s′′∈{0,1,2,3,4}s^{\prime},s^{\prime\prime}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}.

Now, we consider the state in round i+1i+1. Since Q⁡(i,l)Q(i,l) and Q⁡(i−1,l)Q(i-1,l) are coupled and follow the same policy, 𝒟⁡(i,i)=𝒟⁡(i−1,i)\mathcal{D}(i,i)=\mathcal{D}(i-1,i). In round ii, QiQ_{i} follows our policy and Qi−1Q_{i-1} follow the optimal policy, which implies D⁡(i,i)≤D⁡(i−1,i)D(i,i)\leq D(i-1,i) and we split this in two cases:

  1. (case 1’)

    If D⁡(i,i)=0D(i,i)=0 and D⁡(i−1,i)=1D(i-1,i)=1, then round i+1i+1 would be in state Si+1,1S_{i+1,1}. Due to our case analysis above, we have Si+2,0S_{i+2,0} or Si+2,1S_{i+2,1} for round i+2i+2. If the state of round i+2i+2 is Si+2,0S_{i+2,0}, then we have Si′,0S_{i^{\prime},0} for each round i′≥i+2i^{\prime}\geq i+2, in which case ψ⁡(i,t)=0\psi(i,t)=0. If we have Si+2,1S_{i+2,1} for round i+2i+2, we repeat the same argument as for state i+1i+1. If we observe St,1S_{t,1} for round tt, then we have ψ⁡(i,t)=1\psi(i,t)=1. Otherwise, round tt would be in state St,0S_{t,0}, in which case ψ⁡(i,t)=0\psi(i,t)=0.

  2. (case 2’)

    If D⁡(i,i)=D⁡(i−1,i)D(i,i)=D(i-1,i), then round i+1i+1 would be in state Si+1,0S_{i+1,0} or Si+1,3S_{i+1,3}. By our case analysis above, we have Si+2,0S_{i+2,0} or Si+2,2S_{i+2,2} or Si+2,3S_{i+2,3} for round i+2i+2. If the state of round i+2i+2 is Si+2,0S_{i+2,0}, then we have Si′,0S_{i^{\prime},0} for each round i′≥i+2i^{\prime}\geq i+2, in which case ψ⁡(i,t)=0\psi(i,t)=0. If we have Si+2,2S_{i+2,2} for round i+2i+2, we have Si+3,0S_{i+3,0} or Si+3,2S_{i+3,2} for round i+3i+3. If Si+3,0S_{i+3,0} is the state of round i+3i+3, then as before, we deduce ψ⁡(i,t)=0\psi(i,t)=0. If the state is Si+3,2S_{i+3,2}, we repeat the same argument as for state i+2i+2. If we observe St,2S_{t,2} for round tt, then we have ψ⁡(i,t)=−1\psi(i,t)=-1. Otherwise, round tt would be in state St,0S_{t,0}, in which case ψ⁡(i,t)=0\psi(i,t)=0. If we observe Si+2,3S_{i+2,3} for round i+2i+2, then we again repeat the argument as for round i+1i+1 to argue that ψ⁡(i,t)∈{0,−1}\psi(i,t)\in\{0,-1\}.

This finishes the proof.

Notice that M⁡(t)M(t) and τ⁡(t)\tau(t) have circular definition as M⁡(t)M(t) requires τ⁡(t)\tau(t) and τ⁡(t)\tau(t) requires M⁡(t)M(t). Although this is not problematic as both M⁡(t)M(t) and τ⁡(t)\tau(t) are only required in analysis, we avoid this circular definition and remove ambiguity by using the definitions in Equation 7. To check the existence of τ⁡(t)\tau(t) and M⁡(t)M(t), first we can see that M~​(u)\widetilde{M}(u) is monotonically decreasing in uu and τ~​(M)\widetilde{\tau}(M) is monotonically increasing in MM. Therefore τ~​(M~​(u))\widetilde{\tau}(\widetilde{M}(u)) is monotonically decreasing in uu, which means there exists a minimum value of u∈ℕu\in\mathbb{N} such that u≥τ~​(M~​(u))u\geq\widetilde{\tau}(\widetilde{M}(u)) which we define τ⁡(t)\tau(t). Then M⁡(t)M(t) is also defined as M~​(τ​(t))\widetilde{M}(\tau(t)).

Now, by the direct result of Lemma 12, we have

ℙ⁡(N⁡(τ⁡(t))≥M⁡(t))≥1−t−2,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(N(\tau(t))\geq M(t))\geq 1-t^{-2}, (17)

which means we have M⁡(t)M(t) random exploration until round τ⁡(t)\tau(t) with high probability.

Now, we prepare to apply Proposition 39, which shows high probability lower bound of the design matrix VlV_{l} that consists of the i.i.d. sampled features. Recall that our random exploration is done in a round-robin manner. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
